Randomization (Permutation) Test for Two Independent Groups

Source: R/randomization_test.R
randomization_test.Rd

Compares two independent groups by referring the observed statistic to the distribution of that same statistic over reassignments of the observed scores to the two groups. That reference distribution, not a normal or a t distribution, supplies the p-value, so the test needs no assumption about the shape of the population. Alongside the test, the function reports the effect sizes that answer the question the test only screens: the mean difference and its randomization-based interval, the standardized mean difference with a noncentral t interval, the common language effect size, and Cliff's delta.

Usage

randomization_test(
  x = NULL,
  group = NULL,
  data = NULL,
  group_1 = NULL,
  group_2 = NULL,
  statistic = c("mean", "t"),
  alternative = c("two_sided", "less", "greater"),
  exact = NULL,
  n_resamples = 10000L,
  seed = NULL,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  shift_ci = TRUE
)

Arguments

x

A formula of the form y ~ group, or a numeric response vector to be paired with group. Leave NULL when the two samples are supplied through group_1 and group_2.

group

A grouping variable the same length as x, with exactly two levels after unused levels are dropped. Ignored when x is a formula.

data

An optional data.frame in which to find the variables named in the formula.

group_1, group_2

The two samples supplied directly as numeric vectors, an alternative to the formula and response-plus-grouping interfaces. Lengths need not be equal.

statistic

One of "mean" (default) or "t". "mean" uses the difference in group means. "t" uses the studentized (Welch) statistic, which divides that difference by its separate-variances standard error and is the better choice when the groups differ in size and may differ in variance (see Details). The statistic is refused when both observed groups are constant at different values (exactly, or to within the tolerance of the comparison), where its standard error is 0 (see When the studentized statistic is undefined); a reassignment with that property in the reference set of other data is ordered as Inf or -Inf, and when every score is equal the statistic is 0.

alternative

One of "two_sided" (default; the base-R spelling "two.sided" is accepted as an alias), "less", or "greater". The direction refers to the first group minus the second, the same orientation t.test uses.

exact

Logical. If NULL (default), the test enumerates every reassignment when choose(N, n_1) is at most 50,000 and samples reassignments otherwise. If TRUE, enumeration is forced (refused above 1,000,000 reassignments). If FALSE, Monte Carlo is forced.

n_resamples

A single whole number of at least 1: the number of randomly drawn reassignments when enumeration is not used. Default 10000L.

seed

Optional integer seed for the Monte Carlo branch. Default NULL, under which the reassignments are drawn from, and advance, the current random number stream; supply an integer for reproducibility. When a seed is supplied the RNG state in place before the call is restored on exit.

conf_level

Confidence level for every interval reported, the inverted randomization interval included. Default 0.95.

shift_ci

Logical. Compute the randomization-based interval for the shift by inverting the test? Default TRUE. Setting it to FALSE reports the two endpoints as NA and skips the inversion, which is the expensive part of the call.

Value

A data.frame with a term column and a numeric value column, in three blocks.

The test: mean_difference (first group minus second), statistic (the statistic actually referred to the reference distribution, always finite), p_value, and p_value_se (the Monte Carlo standard error of the p-value, NA under exact enumeration, which has no Monte Carlo error).

The intervals and effect sizes: shift_ci_lower and shift_ci_upper (the randomization interval for the shift, obtained by inverting the test); normal_theory_ci_lower and normal_theory_ci_upper (Welch's t interval on the same mean difference, reported for contrast); smd with smd_ci_lower and smd_ci_upper from ci_smd; cles with cles_ci_lower and cles_ci_upper from cles; and cliff_delta with cliff_delta_ci_lower and cliff_delta_ci_upper from cliff_delta. When the pooled within-group variance is zero (each group constant) the standardized mean difference is undefined: the six rows smd, smd_ci_lower, smd_ci_upper, cles, cles_ci_lower, and cles_ci_upper are NA, a warning of class dmar_smd_undefined says so, and the test, the shift interval, and Cliff's delta are reported as usual.

The design: n_1, n_2, N, n_evaluated (how many reassignments were actually used), and exact (1 if every reassignment was enumerated, 0 if they were sampled).

Non-numeric information travels on attributes rather than in the value column: statistic_name, method (“exact enumeration” or “Monte Carlo”), alternative, group_labels, response_name, group_name, seed, observed_statistic, and reference_distribution, the vector of statistics over the reassignments that plot_randomization_test draws, which can hold Inf and -Inf under statistic = "t" (see statistic). reference_extreme is a logical vector of the same length that marks the reassignments the p-value counted as at least as extreme as the observed one.

No table is returned when statistic = "t" is refused; the condition, of class dmar_studentized_statistic_undefined, carries reason ("constant_groups"), alternative, n_1, n_2, and p_value_mean, the exact p-value statistic = "mean" gives for the same data and alternative.

Details

What the randomization distribution is. Suppose N participants were randomly assigned, \(n_1\) to one condition and \(n_2\) to the other. Under the null hypothesis that the condition a participant received made no difference to that participant's score, each score would have been the same number no matter which group the participant landed in. The assignment actually used was one draw from the \(\binom{N}{n_1}\) assignments the randomization could equally well have produced, so every one of those assignments was equally likely, and each of them yields a value of the test statistic. Those values are the randomization distribution. The p-value is the proportion of them at least as extreme as the value the experiment actually produced.

Why there is no normality assumption. Nothing in that argument mentions a population, a normal curve, or a sampling model. The probability comes from the coin flips the experimenter performed, which are known exactly because the experimenter performed them. This is the inferential logic Fisher (1935) used to introduce experimental design, and it is where Chapter 1 of Maxwell, Delaney, and Kelley (2027) starts, for the same reason: the validity of the test rests on the randomization rather than on assumptions a data analyst cannot check.

What the test does and does not license. A small p-value says the observed separation between the groups would rarely arise from reassignment alone, which is evidence that the assignment mattered. It does not say how much it mattered, and with a large N an uninteresting difference will produce a small p-value. It also does not, by itself, license generalization beyond the participants at hand: randomization licenses a causal claim about these units, while generalization to a population is a separate argument that rests on how the units were recruited. That is why this function reports effect sizes with intervals rather than a p-value alone.

Why the studentized statistic. With \(n_1 = n_2\) the separate-variances standard error equals the pooled one, and the pooled t is an increasing function of the mean difference over the reassignments, so the two statistics give the same p-value in every balanced design. They differ only when the groups are unequal in size. Reassigning scores between groups of unequal size mixes the two variances in proportions that the observed assignment does not have, so the reference distribution for the raw mean difference is built under a null that is false in a second way, and the test's actual Type I error rate drifts away from the nominal level. The studentized statistic rescales each reassignment by its own separate-variances standard error, which removes most of that drift and remains asymptotically valid under heteroscedasticity (Janssen, 1997; Neuhaus, 1993). Use statistic = "t" when the group sizes differ and unequal variances are plausible.

When the studentized statistic is undefined. The studentized statistic is a ratio, the difference in means over its standard error, and it has a value only when that standard error is positive. If each group is constant and the two constants differ (exactly, or to within the tolerance of the comparison), the standard error of the observed data is 0 and statistic = "t" is refused with a condition of class dmar_studentized_statistic_undefined. The observed data are then at the boundary of the reference set: among the reassignments only the observed one and, with equal group sizes, the one that exchanges the groups have a zero standard error. The refusal concerns the statistic and not the evidence. statistic = "mean" is defined for every arrangement and gives the smallest p-value the design allows in the direction of the data, \(1/\binom{N}{n_1}\) one-sided, and two-sided \(2/\binom{N}{n_1}\) with equal group sizes and \(1/\binom{N}{n_1}\) otherwise; the message states the value, and the condition carries it as p_value_mean. The refusal is made before any reassignment is enumerated or drawn, so a refused Monte Carlo call leaves the random number stream where it was. With statistic = "mean" the same data return the table, with the warning of class dmar_smd_undefined described under Value.

When the observed statistic is defined, some arrangements in the reference set can still have a zero standard error: with a two-valued outcome, the reassignment that puts every high score in one group. Those arrangements are kept and ordered as the limit of the statistic, Inf or -Inf with the sign of their mean difference, so they count as the most extreme arrangements, which is where the mean difference also places them. Refusing them would refuse ordinary binary and coarsely measured data. For group_1 = c(1, 1, 1, 0) against group_2 = c(0, 0, 0, 1) the reference distribution of the studentized statistic holds one -Inf and one Inf among its 70 values, and the p-value, 34/70, is the one the difference in means gives. When every score is equal, every arrangement is the same data set; the statistic is reported as 0 and the p-value is 1.

Ties. A reassignment whose statistic equals the observed one counts as at least as extreme. Two statistics that are equal in exact arithmetic can differ in their last binary digits as computed, so the comparison allows for the rounding of the arithmetic, with a bound proportional to the size of the scores. Where the bound cannot separate two statistics they are counted as tied, so the p-value can be above the exact one and is not below it. For the difference in means that happens only when two mean differences agree to within about 1e-14 of the largest absolute score, as when scores agree to about fourteen significant digits or one score is about 1e14 times the rest. For the studentized statistic it can also happen when one score is about ten million times the spread of the rest, or when every score lies within about a millionth of one of two values.

Exact or Monte Carlo. When choose(N, n_1) is at most 50,000 every reassignment is enumerated and the p-value is exact: it is a count divided by a known total, with no approximation anywhere. Above that threshold n_resamples reassignments are drawn at random and the p-value is \((r + 1) / (m + 1)\), where r counts the sampled reassignments at least as extreme as the observed one and m is n_resamples. Adding one to each part counts the observed assignment, which is itself a legitimate reassignment; without it a p-value of exactly zero could be reported for a hypothesis the data cannot rule out, and the test would be anticonservative (Phipson & Smyth, 2010). The reported p_value_se is \(\sqrt{\hat p (1 - \hat p) / m}\), the standard error of the resampling itself. It describes how much the p-value would move if the reassignments were drawn again, not how much it would move in a new experiment. Raising n_resamples shrinks it at the usual \(1/\sqrt{m}\) rate.

The randomization interval, and how it differs from the normal theory one. Suppose the treatment adds a constant \(\delta\) to every score it touches. Subtracting \(\delta\) from each first-group score should then leave scores that are exchangeable across groups, so the randomization test applied to the subtracted data is a test of \(H_0\!: \mathrm{shift} = \delta\). The set of \(\delta\) for which that test does not reject at level \(1 - \) conf_level is a confidence interval for the shift, and it is reported as shift_ci_lower and shift_ci_upper. Inverting a test this way is the general recipe (Ernst, 2004); the endpoints are located by bisection on the p-value, using the same reassignments throughout so the interval and the test agree.

The contrast with normal_theory_ci_lower and normal_theory_ci_upper, which are Welch's t limits on the same mean difference, is worth reading whenever both are printed. The randomization interval is exactly the set of shifts the test being run does not reject, so the test and the interval can never disagree. The normal theory interval instead assumes the sampling distribution of the mean difference has a known shape; it is smooth, symmetric about the point estimate, and can extend past the range the data can support. The randomization interval is discrete, need not be symmetric, and in a very small design is unbounded, a correct statement of how little information the design carries rather than a defect: with three observations per group the smallest attainable two-sided p-value is 2/20 = 0.10, so no shift can be rejected at the 5% level and the 95% interval is the whole real line. The randomization interval also inherits the shift model, so it answers a narrower question than the test does: the test needs only exchangeability, while the interval needs the treatment to move every score by the same amount.

Effect sizes. Every effect size reported here comes from the package function that owns it, so the numbers match a direct call. The one exception is a pooled within-group variance of zero, where the standardized mean difference and the common language effect size are reported as NA (see Value). smd and ci_smd supply the standardized mean difference and its noncentral t interval; cles supplies the common language effect size, the probability that a randomly drawn score from the first group exceeds one from the second, by transforming those limits through \(\Phi(\cdot/\sqrt 2)\); and cliff_delta supplies Cliff's delta with its consistent interval. The standardized mean difference and the common language effect size are normal theory quantities, so their intervals lean on the assumption the test itself avoids. Cliff's delta does not: it is a function of the ordering of the observations alone, which makes it the natural effect size companion to a randomization test. Reporting all three lets a reader see whether the distribution-free and normal theory summaries tell the same story.

Ranks give the Wilcoxon test. Replacing the scores by their ranks and running this test with statistic = "mean" reproduces the exact Wilcoxon rank sum test, since the rank sum is a monotone function of the difference in mean ranks. That equivalence is a useful check and a reminder of what the rank test is: a randomization test on transformed data.

References

Edgington, E. S., & Onghena, P. (2007). Randomization tests (4th ed.). Chapman & Hall/CRC.

Ernst, M. D. (2004). Permutation methods: A basis for exact inference. Statistical Science, 19(4), 676–685. doi:10.1214/088342304000000396

Fisher, R. A. (1935). The design of experiments. Oliver & Boyd.

Janssen, A. (1997). Studentized permutation tests for non-i.i.d. hypotheses and the generalized Behrens-Fisher problem. Statistics & Probability Letters, 36(1), 9–21. doi:10.1016/S0167-7152(97)00043-6

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge. (See Chapter 1 on the logic of randomization and the randomization test.)

Neuhaus, G. (1993). Conditional rank tests for the two-sample problem under random censorship. The Annals of Statistics, 21(4), 1760–1779. doi:10.1214/aos/1176349396

Phipson, B., & Smyth, G. K. (2010). Permutation p-values should never be zero: Calculating exact p-values when permutations are randomly drawn. Statistical Applications in Genetics and Molecular Biology, 9(1), Article 39. doi:10.2202/1544-6115.1585

Pitman, E. J. G. (1937). Significance tests which may be applied to samples from any populations. Supplement to the Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, 4(1), 119–130.

Examples

# 1. Ten observations, so every one of the choose(10, 5) = 252
#    reassignments is enumerated and the p-value is exact.
treatment <- c(80, 84, 79, 88, 83)
control   <- c(72, 75, 68, 81, 74)
randomization_test(group_1 = treatment, group_2 = control)
#>  term                   value 
#>  mean_difference        8.800 
#>  statistic              8.800 
#>  p_value                0.0238
#>  p_value_se             <NA>  
#>  shift_ci_lower         3.000 
#>  shift_ci_upper         15.000
#>  normal_theory_ci_lower 2.598 
#>  normal_theory_ci_upper 15.002
#>  smd                    2.098 
#>  smd_ci_lower           0.461 
#>  smd_ci_upper           3.659 
#>  cles                   0.931 
#>  cles_ci_lower          0.628 
#>  cles_ci_upper          0.995 
#>  cliff_delta            0.840 
#>  cliff_delta_ci_lower   -0.117
#>  cliff_delta_ci_upper   0.988 
#>  n_1                    5     
#>  n_2                    5     
#>  N                      10    
#>  n_evaluated            252   
#>  exact                  1     
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# 2. The studentized statistic. The groups are the same size here, so it
#    gives the same p-value as the difference in means; the two differ
#    when the groups are unequal in size.
randomization_test(group_1 = treatment, group_2 = control,
                   statistic = "t")
#>  term                   value 
#>  mean_difference        8.800 
#>  statistic              3.317 
#>  p_value                0.0238
#>  p_value_se             <NA>  
#>  shift_ci_lower         3.000 
#>  shift_ci_upper         15.000
#>  normal_theory_ci_lower 2.598 
#>  normal_theory_ci_upper 15.002
#>  smd                    2.098 
#>  smd_ci_lower           0.461 
#>  smd_ci_upper           3.659 
#>  cles                   0.931 
#>  cles_ci_lower          0.628 
#>  cles_ci_upper          0.995 
#>  cliff_delta            0.840 
#>  cliff_delta_ci_lower   -0.117
#>  cliff_delta_ci_upper   0.988 
#>  n_1                    5     
#>  n_2                    5     
#>  N                      10    
#>  n_evaluated            252   
#>  exact                  1     
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# 3. Formula interface: weekly drinking in the two comparable arms of
#    the drinks_trial data, a right-skewed outcome, which is exactly
#    where a distribution-free test earns its keep. With 37 and 32
#    participants there are far too many reassignments to enumerate, so
#    they are drawn at random and the p-value carries a Monte Carlo
#    standard error. n_resamples = 2000 keeps the example quick; a
#    reported p-value deserves the default of 10,000.
cra <- droplevels(subset(drinks_trial, treatment != "CRA + Disulfiram"))
set.seed(113)
randomization_test(drinks_per_week ~ treatment, data = cra,
                   n_resamples = 2000, seed = 113)
#>  term                   value  
#>  mean_difference        24.474 
#>  statistic              24.474 
#>  p_value                0.2804 
#>  p_value_se             0.010  
#>  shift_ci_lower         -13.102
#>  shift_ci_upper         63.998 
#>  normal_theory_ci_lower -15.802
#>  normal_theory_ci_upper 64.749 
#>  smd                    0.282  
#>  smd_ci_lower           -0.195 
#>  smd_ci_upper           0.756  
#>  cles                   0.579  
#>  cles_ci_lower          0.445  
#>  cles_ci_upper          0.704  
#>  cliff_delta            0.300  
#>  cliff_delta_ci_lower   0.021  
#>  cliff_delta_ci_upper   0.535  
#>  n_1                    37     
#>  n_2                    32     
#>  N                      69     
#>  n_evaluated            2000   
#>  exact                  0      
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# 4. A one-sided test, and the one-sided interval that goes with it.
randomization_test(group_1 = treatment, group_2 = control,
                   alternative = "greater")
#>  term                   value 
#>  mean_difference        8.800 
#>  statistic              8.800 
#>  p_value                0.0119
#>  p_value_se             <NA>  
#>  shift_ci_lower         4.000 
#>  shift_ci_upper         Inf   
#>  normal_theory_ci_lower 3.816 
#>  normal_theory_ci_upper Inf   
#>  smd                    2.098 
#>  smd_ci_lower           0.461 
#>  smd_ci_upper           3.659 
#>  cles                   0.931 
#>  cles_ci_lower          0.628 
#>  cles_ci_upper          0.995 
#>  cliff_delta            0.840 
#>  cliff_delta_ci_lower   -0.117
#>  cliff_delta_ci_upper   0.988 
#>  n_1                    5     
#>  n_2                    5     
#>  N                      10    
#>  n_evaluated            252   
#>  exact                  1     
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# 5. On ranks, the test is the exact Wilcoxon rank sum test.
y <- c(treatment, control)
g <- rep(c("treatment", "control"), each = 5)
res <- randomization_test(rank(y), g)
res$value[res$term == "p_value"]
#> [1] 0.03174603
wilcox.test(treatment, control, exact = TRUE)$p.value
#> [1] 0.03174603

# 6. Both observed groups are constant, at different values. The
#    difference in means is defined, and gives the smallest p-value
#    groups of 4 and 4 allow. The warnings say that the standardized
#    mean difference is undefined and that the groups do not overlap.
#    With statistic = "t" the same call is refused, with a message that
#    says why: the standard error is 0, so the studentized statistic is
#    undefined.
randomization_test(group_1 = rep(5, 4), group_2 = rep(3, 4))
#> Warning: The standardized mean difference and the common language effect size are undefined because the pooled within-group variance is zero; the randomization test and Cliff's delta are reported.
#> Warning: randomization_test(): for the Cliff's delta rows (computed by cliff_delta()), the groups are completely separated (|delta| = 1), so the estimated variance is 0. Both confidence limits are reported equal to the estimate (1, 1). They are not a confidence interval with the stated coverage: the variance estimate is built from how much the comparisons differ from one observation to the next, and in a sample with no overlap they do not differ at all. That describes this sample, not the population. A population with some overlap often produces a sample with none when the samples are small (here 4 and 4 observations), so the limits must not be read as showing that the population value is 1. For this case Feng and Cliff (2004, Equation 8) give the limit (n_b - z^2) / (n_b + z^2) for delta, with n_b the smaller group size and z the normal quantile of the level: 0.020 here at the 95% level, with the other limit 1. Report the estimate with the sample sizes and say that the groups did not overlap; the randomization test (randomization_test()) gives a p-value that remains valid here.
#>  term                   value 
#>  mean_difference        2.000 
#>  statistic              2.000 
#>  p_value                0.0286
#>  p_value_se             <NA>  
#>  shift_ci_lower         2.000 
#>  shift_ci_upper         2.000 
#>  normal_theory_ci_lower <NA>  
#>  normal_theory_ci_upper <NA>  
#>  smd                    <NA>  
#>  smd_ci_lower           <NA>  
#>  smd_ci_upper           <NA>  
#>  cles                   <NA>  
#>  cles_ci_lower          <NA>  
#>  cles_ci_upper          <NA>  
#>  cliff_delta            1.000 
#>  cliff_delta_ci_lower   1.000 
#>  cliff_delta_ci_upper   1.000 
#>  n_1                    4     
#>  n_2                    4     
#>  N                      8     
#>  n_evaluated            70    
#>  exact                  1     
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
